newsitem.title: USA: Spacewalkers begin Hubble service call.
newsitem.headline: Spacewalkers begin Hubble service call.

text.p: After a last-minute delay, two astronauts floated outside the shuttle Discovery late on Thursday on the first of four spacewalks to service the Hubble Space Telescope.

Astronauts Mark Lee and Steve Smith, wearing bulky white spacesuits, climbed out into the shuttle's open cargo bay at about 11:45 p.m. EST (0445 GMT) as the shuttle soared 360 miles (575 km) above Australia.
"Oh my gosh, beautiful," said Smith as he floated outside with the gleaming, sliver observatory towering overhead. "Wow, look at that telescope," added Lee.
The spacewalk, to fit Hubble with two new scientific instruments, was held up for one hour, 45 minutes after one of the telescope's two fragile solar arrays swung round violently and unexpectedly.

"We saw something real unusual," Discovery crewman Joe Tanner told mission control. "The ... array skewed from horizontal to vertical and then about halfway back to horizontal." The rapid movement of the 40-foot 12-metre-long panel occurred in just five seconds, he said.
"That must have been very dramatic," mission control's Jeff Hoffman replied.
The incident occurred at 9:45 p.m. EST (0245 GMT) as Lee and Smith prepared to leave the shuttle's airlock.

Flight controllers said air vented overboard from the airlock compartment, which for the first time was mounted in the cargo bay, had struck the panel and set it moving. The delicate arrays appeared unharmed by the incident, they said.
During the six-hour spacewalk, the two men were to fit the telescope with an infrared camera and an improved spectrometer, the main goals of the shuttle's $350 million service call.

The $105 million multipurpose infrared camera, known as NICMOS, will allow astronomers to see deeper into the universe than ever before and may discover planets orbiting other stars, while a $125 million improved spectrograph, called STIS, will help in the search for massive black holes devouring stars in the centre of galaxies.
The new instruments, both about the size of a refrigerator, will replace two ageing spectrographs, one of which suffered a power failure a few days before the shuttle's launch.

Upgrades planned during spacewalks over the following three days included the installation of a new digital tape recorder, a more accurate guidance sensor for pointing the telescope and various improved electronic boxes.
It was the first time astronauts had worked on the $2 billion orbiting observatory since the 1993 repair that fixed its blurred vision.
